source.title: Mapping the evidence on dual-task training in musculoskeletal injury rehabilitation: a systematic review

paper.citation: Akkus C, Pakoz B, Gultekinler BD, Turgut E. Mapping the evidence on dual-task training in musculoskeletal injury rehabilitation: a systematic review. Research in Sports Medicine. 2026:1–36. doi:10.1080/15438627.2026.2673035.
paper.abstract: This preregistered systematic review mapped randomized evidence for repeated motor-cognitive or motor-motor dual-task training in adult musculoskeletal rehabilitation. Eight trials involving 224 adults covered ankle instability, ACL reconstruction, knee ligament-dominance deficit, and elbow fracture. Heterogeneity prevented quantitative pooling, so the authors used a best-evidence synthesis.
paper.tldr: Dual-task rehabilitation can improve selected outcomes, but the clearest ACL-reconstruction evidence indicates results comparable to single-task training rather than superior. The small, heterogeneous evidence base does not establish better return-to-sport or reinjury outcomes.
paper.methods: The review included peer-reviewed English or Turkish randomized trials in adults aged 18–65 years that compared repeated dual-task rehabilitation with single-task training, usual care, or no intervention. The authors assessed risk of bias and graded condition-specific consistency using a best-evidence framework because injuries, interventions, comparators, and outcomes were too heterogeneous for meta-analysis.
paper.findings: Eight trials included 224 adults, and four trials were rated high risk of bias. Strong evidence indicated comparable postural-control and patient-reported improvements from dual- and single-task training after ACL reconstruction. Moderate evidence indicated dual-task training was comparable to single-task training and superior to no intervention for selected ankle-instability outcomes. Evidence for several proprioceptive, neuromuscular, and kinematic outcomes was conflicting or limited.
paper.limitations: Only eight small trials were included, half were high risk of bias, and outcome measurement was a recurring concern. Evidence was concentrated in lower-extremity conditions, interventions lasted 4–12 weeks, and long-term retention, reinjury, and return-to-sport outcomes were not established. Database and language restrictions may have omitted relevant studies.
paper.practicalImplications: Use dual-task progressions when the secondary demand matches a meaningful rehabilitation objective and the athlete can maintain movement quality. Do not assume that adding cognitive load is inherently superior; compare it with a clear single-task baseline and monitor task-specific response.
paper.athleteDev: Progress from stable single-task execution to controlled secondary demands that reflect the athlete's sport and decision environment. Preserve technical quality and expose complexity deliberately rather than using dual-task difficulty as a generic marker of readiness.
paper.rtp: The review does not validate a dual-task clearance test or show reduced reinjury. Dual-task performance may contribute contextual information during late-stage rehabilitation, but it should sit alongside tissue recovery, strength, power, movement, exposure, symptoms, and sport-specific progression.
